articles.title: Bruce Buffer finds Josh Hokit disrespectful #ufc
articles.description: Josh Hokit has made his feelings known, but Chael Sonnen believes there's a harsh reality he needs to understand about the fight business. Chael breaks down Hokit's comments about his importance to the UFC and why he believes the attitude comes across as disrespectful. In MMA, a fighter's value can change quickly. A couple of bad results can mean a different paycheck, a lower spot on the card, and a much shorter path to the exit. Meanwhile, Chael points out that Bruce Buffer's future earning power looks very different from a fighter's. It's a reminder that being part of the UFC doesn't guarantee long-term security. Hokit has pushed back against the criticism, bringing up the bad guys and criminals who have been part of the fight game. But will that response help his case? Chael explains why the business of fighting can be unforgiving — and why a fighter's next performance can matter more than he realizes. Subscribe for more Chael Sonnen analysis, UFC news, and MMA commentary. #JoshHokit #ChaelSonnen #UFC #BruceBuffer #MMA #UFCNews

articles.title: Charles Won't Change His Style for the BMF
articles.description: Use my code CHAEL to get up to 50% off your Hume Pod: https://sponsr.is/humehealth_chael #HumeHealth #smartscale #weightloss Charles Oliveira beat Max Holloway for the BMF belt, and a loud part of the fanbase decided he fought the wrong way: too much of the fight on the ground, not enough standing in the middle and slugging. The call was actually made that he should give the belt back. Oliveira's answer was simple: he is not changing his style because he is fighting for the BMF belt, and Chael Sonnen says he is right. Chael traces the style argument back to where it started, 1993, when the UFC was formed and nobody actually knew whether wrestling, boxing, or grappling was the best way to win a fight. It got settled then, and it has been settled ever since: you bring every tool you have, and the whole thing has always been about who can beat up the other guy. But that leaves the real question. If the BMF is not about record, and it is not about style, what is it? Chael's answer: veteran status, and you will know it when you see it. Cub Swanson is a BMF. The Diaz brothers and Jorge Masvidal obviously are. Diego Lopes changes what the word means. And if the matchmakers want a guaranteed slugfest, that is a booking problem, not a fighter problem. Book Mike Perry. He will give you one. articles.title: What Really Drives Alexander Volkanovski
articles.description: The story of Alexander Volkanovski is not being told accurately, and Chael Sonnen is going to fix that. Volk is the one champion with real leverage behind the scenes who has never once used it. He has never tried to renegotiate, never tried to get out of a fight, and where every other champion angles for the biggest paycheck against the easiest opponent, Volkanovski goes out of his way to fight the hardest guy available. Movsar Evloev is 19-0 and has beaten former world champions, and Volk asked for him anyway. Now Volk says he will stop Evloev, then he wants Justin Gaethje. Chael says the Gaethje fight is not coming, and explains why that does not matter: people have been calling Volkanovski's next fight his last one for three years, Daniel Cormier was once prepared to give him a retirement send-off on commentary, and the thing still driving Volk is the one thing he has never done. Along the way, Chael makes the point every fighter needs to hear: nobody remembers your record, not even the fighters themselves. The most valuable thing a win gives you is not the belt. It is a platform, and Volk is positioned to use his. Chapters: 0:00 The Volkanovski story isn't being told accurately 0:30 The champion with leverage who never uses it 1:13 He goes out of his way to fight the hardest guy 2:00 Evloev is 19-0 and has beaten former champions 2:40 "I'll stop him. Then I'm going to fight Justin Gaethje." 3:08 Why the Gaethje fight isn't coming 3:46 Three years of "this is Volk's last fight" 4:34 The one thing he's never done is still driving him 5:37 Nobody remembers your record. Chael doesn't know his own. 7:12 The most important thing a win gives you is a platform 8:42 Calling out Gaethje is a gangster move #ChaelSonnen #AlexanderVolkanovski #UFC #MMA #Featherweight

articles.title: Dricus Du Plessis Is Getting in His Own Way
articles.description: Nobody has ever played the promotion game better than Dricus Du Plessis, and Chael Sonnen can prove it. Dricus was an interchangeable undercard fighter until he did the one thing nobody else would do: he complained. When Bo Nickal got better card placement than him, Dricus spoke up, and when a slot opened, the UFC went straight to the only guy who asked for it. He beat Darren Till, talked his way into a co-main event, and knocked off Robert Whittaker as a 2.5-to-1 underdog. That parlayed into a world title and one of the hottest feuds the sport has ever seen. But since the Khamzat Chimaev loss, Dricus has gone quiet, and Chael says that is the one mistake a guy like him cannot make. Now Dricus says he cuts 45 pounds to make middleweight, wants his belt back at 185, and then wants the light heavyweight title too. Chael explains why that exact path did not work the way people remember for Alex Pereira, why the Chimaev matchup is simply a bad one for him, and why if Dricus wants 205, the time is right now, not after another run at a belt he plans to leave behind. Chapters: 0:00 The squeaky wheel: how Dricus talked his way off the undercard 2:00 He beat Whittaker, and the hottest feud in the sport was born 3:33 The Chimaev loss, and why going quiet is the one mistake he can't make 4:13 A main event with Kamaru Usman, off a loss 5:19 The Strickland argument: "I beat the champion twice" 6:20 Cutting 45 pounds, and the 185-then-205 plan 6:46 The Pereira story everybody tells wrong 8:02 If you want 205, go now 8:17 Some matchups are just bad matchups #ChaelSonnen #DricusDuPlessis #UFC #MMA #Middleweight

articles.title: Does the UFC Secretly Love Josh Hokit?
articles.description: Ask Uncle Chael is back, and this week's questions hit everything: marriage, folkstyle, a fight Chael says was stopped on a tap that never happened, and whether the UFC hates Josh Hokit. Jeff Finnegan leads off: should I have kids? Then CJS sets a wrestling round robin between Spencer Lee, Ono, and Roman Bravo-Young, and somebody has to go 0-2. Anthony asks whether to lock in on fitness and his own business first or find a wife at the same time, and Chael flips the order entirely: the wife is the one you want the most, and you do all of it at once. BOD asks why folkstyle is not popular on the world scene, and Chael explains why the American style no other country wrestles may be exactly why Americans run MMA. A fan asks about a fourth fight with Jeremy Horn, Eric Sands asks whether a man proving everyone wrong is living on his enemies' terms, and Chael tells the Florida story: Trevor Prangley, a submission stoppage he says he never tapped to, and a brutal locker-room interrogation by the commission. Plus why every great story needs a villain, why David Robert Web's geography numbers are fake news, and the Hokit question: Ciryl Gane got the promo video, Hokit got no mention, so does the UFC hate him? Chael's answer is a list of everything the UFC has handed him. The final question is a fan's top five UFC fighters of all time, and Chael wants the gold, silver, and bronze medals for himself. articles.title: Bruce Buffer Crossed a Line With Josh Hokit
articles.description: Bruce Buffer weighed in on Josh Hokit, and Chael Sonnen says it breaks the one rule production people are never supposed to break. To explain it, he tells the Arianny Celeste story, and the phone call that taught him how this business actually works. After the first Anderson Silva fight, Chael was told Arianny had said she was glad it happened to him, for all the trash he talked. He fired back. Then came the call: why did you go after her? She is off limits. There is a separation. Fighters on one side, production on the other, and the people paid to make fighters look good stay completely unbiased. The twist: Arianny never said it. She was innocent, and Chael clears her completely. The point stands anyway. Now Bruce. Chael puts it at a one out of ten, and thinks Buffer was actually trying to put Hokit over, then hedged with "I don't agree with everything he says" to keep his own hands clean, the same trap that ended Trent Lott. But look at the asymmetry. Hokit does not know when his next paycheck is, and two bad nights can end his career. Five years from now Bruce is still clearing seven figures, and if Bruce does not show up tonight, business does not change. If Josh does not, it does. And Hokit answered: this game licenses criminals and men fresh out of prison, while he has a degree, All-American honors, a family, and a spotless record, and he is outworking Ciryl Gane at the media game. Why is the announcer the one bringing him down? The closing: Chael softens it. Bruce really did not say anything that bad, it just was not nice and was not meant to elevate Hokit; it looked like Buffer wanted to disassociate himself. And if you want to be in the cage fighting business without getting your hands dirty, who exactly do you disassociate with? Chael remembers when people tried to disassociate from Joe Rogan: it disgusted him, he has not forgiven any of them, and he would not trust or do business with a single one, because they showed him who they are. His prediction: you will never hear about this again, it goes away. But Hokit is not a good guy to come after. If you come after him, you are going to take a bump, and when you do, you need to know you had it coming. 0:00 The Arianny story Chael has to tell first 0:51 The call: she's off limits, there's a separation 1:35 The twist, she never said it 2:25 Production makes fighters look good, and stays unbiased 3:04 Now we have Bruce Buffer and Josh Hokit 3:38 A one out of ten, but it still happened 4:23 Buffer tried to put him over, then covered himself 4:37 The Trent Lott lesson: association gets your hands dirty 6:30 Josh doesn't know when his next paycheck is 6:50 Bruce will clear seven figures either way 7:34 Hokit answers: criminals get licenses in this game 8:05 A degree, an All-American, and never in trouble 8:53 Bruce really didn't say anything that bad 9:09 If you don't want dirty hands, who do you disassociate with? 9:22 The Rogan lesson: Chael remembers who walked away 9:54 Prediction: you'll never hear about it again #UFC #MMA #JoshHokit

His first pick for Paddy is Max Holloway: no good guy, no bad guy, closer in age than you think, and a prediction that flips depending on whether it is three rounds or five. His second pick is Charles Oliveira, the personal-feud fight. Then the title picture comes apart. Charles believes a win over Lopes earns him a title shot, and Chael pushes back on his complaint about Justin Gaethje getting them: Charles, you are the champion right now. articles.title: Cejudo Called Pereira Spoiled. Is He Right?
articles.description: Henry Cejudo says Alex Pereira is spoiled with opportunities, and that he needs to go win two or three more fights before he talks about another title. Chael Sonnen walks the whole career back and asks a simple question: what kind of favor is that? Chael remembers the first time he saw Pereira. Second UFC fight, jerking the curtain at Madison Square Garden in front of almost nobody, doing the bow and arrow, a 36-year-old kickboxer everybody said would fail. He got in the door on his history with Israel Adesanya, then fought on undercards for ten and ten, five different times, in fights even his fans never watched. To even reach Adesanya he had to beat Sean Strickland in a non-main event. He lost four rounds of the title fight, heard his own corner on a hot mic, stayed calm, walked Adesanya down and finished him. Then he gave the rematch away and lost the belt, which turned out to be the gift: freedom from killing himself to make 185. At 38, his light heavyweight debut was Jan Blachowicz, a former champion, won by split decision. His reward for always saying yes was more asks: a short-notice Prochazka rematch, then Salt Lake City against the number eight guy, hurt and sick, telling nobody. He moved to heavyweight for Jon Jones and got a monster kickboxer instead. Now he is 40, in a division he has yet to win, chasing the man who beat him. Spoiled? That is the hardest road in the sport. 0:00 Cejudo's hot take: you're spoiled with opportunities 0:21 Is he right? articles.title: Ilia Topuria Hasn't Said a Word...
articles.description: Ilia Topuria has not said a word, and Chael Sonnen says that silence might be the smartest marketing move in MMA right now. Chael starts with Brock Lesnar, the one monster Vince McMahon would not let speak, because monsters do not talk. Paul Heyman did the talking for him. From there, Chael explains why marketing is never a guarantee, it is an experiment, and sometimes the accident wins. Nick Diaz no-showing the Georges St-Pierre press conference left an empty chair that Dana White thought had ruined the event. It became one of the most successful press conferences of all time. Topuria is running the same play right now, whether he knows it or not. He might be the hottest name at 155 pounds, maybe in all of MMA, and he can pick his opponent and his date. Paddy Pimblett is chasing him and playing it perfectly, but Chael explains why Topuria gains nothing by answering. The fight is huge either way. Then Chael asks the question nobody in the community has suggested out loud: what if Topuria is thinking about retiring? The money, the two-division world titles, the short career, it is all there. And saying it out loud might be exactly the prod that gets him talking. Watch to the end, then tell us in the comments: is the silence strategy, or is it an accident?
